conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for making time to talk with me today. I’m Dr. Carter, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and to help you feel supported in these first weeks and months with your new baby.  

To do that, I’d like to walk through a quick screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s just ten short questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays completely confidential within your care team. My only goal is to understand how you’re coping so we can make sure you’re getting the care you deserve.

When you’re ready, we’ll go through the questions one by one. I’ll ask them conversationally, and you can answer in your own words. If at any point you need to pause or clarify something, just let me know.

Shall we begin?

Thinking about the past week, overall have you been able to enjoy things—little moments, big moments, anything at all—or has that felt pretty difficult lately?

I’ve noticed it’s been hard to really enjoy much lately. Even when I try to do things I used to like—watching a show or stepping outside for a walk—I feel kind of flat, like the color’s been drained out. I still smile at the baby, but it doesn’t come with that warm rush people talk about; it feels more like I’m going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I’ve laughed a little—mostly when my partner makes a joke or when the baby makes a silly face—but it feels forced, like I’m pretending. The sound of my own laugh surprises me, because inside I still feel heavy.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. When I think about tomorrow, or next week, it just feels like more stuff I have to get through. I used to plan little things—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now even those sound exhausting. I don’t feel excited about anything; it’s more like I’m bracing myself.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty much every day. If the baby spits up a lot, I immediately think it’s because I ate the “wrong” thing. When she wouldn’t settle last night, I kept replaying every little choice—did I hold her too long, not long enough? I know rationally it’s not all my fault, but the voice in my head still says I should be doing better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most of the time. Even when everything looks fine on the outside, my mind races—what if she stops breathing when I blink? I’ll check the monitor every few minutes, convinced I’ll see her chest isn’t moving. Sometimes there’s no clear trigger at all; I just feel this tight knot in my stomach like something bad is about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart races, I can’t catch my breath, and I feel shaky, even if the baby’s sleeping peacefully. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me jittery and checking every lock, every blanket, like I’m bracing for something awful I can’t name.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. Most days feel like I’m drowning in small tasks—feeding, changing, trying to sleep, starting all over. I’ll sit down for a second and my mind spins with everything still undone. Sometimes I just stare at the mess and cry because I can’t see how I’ll ever catch up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening almost every night. I’ll finally get the baby down, crawl into bed myself, but my head won’t stop buzzing—replaying every little thing I think I messed up, worrying about what tomorrow will bring. Even when I do drift off, I jerk awake at the tiniest sound, heart pounding, sure something’s wrong.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s a gray cloud hanging over me—even when the baby coos or my partner brings me coffee, the sadness is still right there under the surface. Some afternoons I just sit in the rocking chair with her against my chest and tears slide down for no one clear reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes—three or four times since last weekend. Yesterday it hit while I was folding her tiny onesies; I just started sobbing over a milk stain I couldn’t get out. It feels like the tears come faster than the reasons sometimes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 weeks postpartum, self-referred for mood assessment.

Responses to EPDS-10 (verbatim themes):
- Loss of pleasure/interest: “feels forced,” “exhausting,” “bracing myself”  
- Persistent low mood & crying: “gray cloud,” tears “for no clear reason,” 3–4 crying spells/week  
- Guilt/worthlessness: daily self-blame over infant care; “should be doing better”  
- Anxiety/panic: “mind races,” “tight knot,” “wave” of palpitations 3× this week, no clear trigger  
- Sleep disturbance: difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep unrelated to infant needs  
- Feeling overwhelmed: “drowning in small tasks,” “can’t see how I’ll ever catch up”  
- Appetite/energy: not queried in EPDS; patient did not endorse self-harm ideation (Q10 = 0)

Screening Significance  
Elevated depressive & anxiety symptoms consistent with possible major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety.  
No current self-harm thoughts; safety plan reviewed.

Risk factors noted: primiparous, sleep deprivation, excessive guilt, panic spells, impaired coping.

Recommendation: Formal clinical interview (DSM-5 criteria) and consideration of referral to perinatal mental-health specialty / therapy services; safety reassessment at each contact.
